brief.analysis: Defense has structurally re-rated on a durable rise in global and European military spending, and the data confirms the mean itself is moving: the trend-adjusted reading (barely stretched) diverges sharply from the raw reading, direct evidence the average is drifting up rather than the ratio being temporarily rich. The engine itself left the downturn unconfirmed, and only 3 of 7 past episodes reached target — a poor forward hit rate. The old 5-year average is a stale, too-low target; short this and you are fighting a rising baseline, not a rubber band.
brief.report_line: We are flagged short defense-versus-stocks but advise against it: the fair level has structurally risen with sustained defense budgets, the downtrend is unconfirmed, and past episodes reverted less than half the time.

brief.analysis: Chips have run far ahead of the broader Nasdaq on a genuine, multi-year AI spending boom, so the old 5-year average — which implies a 64% collapse — is an invalid target and clearly a trap. The honest read is that both the raw stretch and the trend-adjusted stretch still agree chips are expensive right now, so a partial pullback toward the 200-day average (about 11% away) is tradeable. Size this down: you are fading a powerful secular trend, and only the modest 200-day target is credible, never the 5-year mean.
brief.report_line: We are short chips-versus-Nasdaq for a partial reversion to the 200-day average only, sized down because the AI-capex boom has permanently raised the fair level and the 5-year mean is unreachable.

brief.analysis: Miners and metals have been lifted by real structural forces — electrification and copper demand plus a stronger gold complex — so part of this move is a genuine re-rating rather than pure froth, keeping the 5-year average as a questionable target. That said, the near-term picture is cleaner than defense: the 200-day target is already met and the ratio is only mildly rich against its own trend. The catch is that the forward hit rate rests on just two past episodes, too thin to lean on hard, so take the reversion to the 200-day average but keep size modest.
brief.report_line: We are short metals-and-miners-versus-stocks for a reversion to the 200-day average that is already in hand, sized modestly because structural metals demand and a two-episode track record limit conviction beyond that.

brief.analysis: The strongest regime argument is that heavy central-bank gold buying has lifted gold's long-run trend, so the flat 5-year average understates where gold-versus-stocks should sit. But that argument actually helps this short: measured against its own rising trend the ratio is now slightly cheap, not rich, and the sensible near-term target (the 200-day average) has already been reached. The full 5-year mean is a stale, too-low target, but the desk isn't aiming there — the tradeable snap-back is essentially done and low-risk.
brief.report_line: We are short gold-versus-stocks into a completed snap-back to its 200-day average; the main risk is that persistent central-bank gold demand keeps gold's trend rising, which is why we do not chase the deeper 5-year target.

brief.analysis: The regime worry is that silver's industrial demand (solar, electronics) has structurally re-rated it against gold, which would lift the long-run silver/gold relationship. That concern is muted here: the violent overshoot (silver having run enormously ahead of gold) has already reverted, the 200-day target is met, and against its own trend the ratio is only mildly rich. The near-term reversion is clean and largely complete; the deeper 5-year target is secondary and less certain.
brief.report_line: We are short silver-versus-gold after an extreme overshoot has already snapped back to its 200-day average; residual risk is silver's structural industrial demand, so we do not press toward the 5-year mean.
